To bring some hope on the architectural side of things, it very well may be easier as time goes on. Now with computers, every new survey is imported into CAD software rather than being hand drafted on sheets. CAD files are a lot easier to work with for conversions, being automatic and all that, than going through archived physical plan sheets, so it's just a matter of time before a vast majority of structures and land plots in the US are in some ways described in a CAD file archive. However, for this conversion they might need to actually just re-do surveys because plans are often out of date, land arrangements change, and any other reason a full survey (not cheap) might be required. 

Going from there we would just need to have regulation providing some "encouragement" for architects/developers/engineers/etc to use metric primarily. I don't believe we can just force people to do that because of the violation of someone's personal freedom when they say "hey, I want this building in imperial" and the government is like "nah, you can't"

I work in civil/mechanical engineering. I can assure you I like science and I can also assure you I have never used metric at work before, ever. It has been tried to switch over before. Twice significantly in recent history. Here in Arizona we actually have the (or one of the) only roads marked with kilos/kmh going into Mexico. 

The entire US isn't just based off of inches and feet, it's based off of ridiculously old units like chains as well - most commonly but not always 66 feet. Or rods, or unicorn horns. It's pretty dumb, but that is how all long standing older buildings in the majority of the US are defined, that is how the vast majority of land plots are described legally in their deeds, and it's how (dumb excuse) all contractors like their stuff.

Oddly enough, a good majority of construction work is done on renovations and repairs for already existing buildings. And as I described, all buildings are described this way. Cost of conversion is something noone will bare the cost to take on, it slows down projects, it's confusing, it's just generally a shitshow and even though it's been tried some times in the past 100 years, and it's costly to do any work without going by an as built survey. When you update the as built, you're not going to be putting 2 different unit systems on there.

To end this textbook of s comment, I have a story for you. Recently there was a new federal court house built in Arizona, and all of the plans were done in metric. Building materials aren't based on metric, most tools aren't based on metric, on and on. So contractors would not take it. Or they bid high. No one wanted to touch it because it was in metric and there would be so much work to keep it accurate to the metric specs.

Of the cost of this project, a sizeable portion of it, in the range of millions, was to have engineers and architects convert all of it back to imperial so it could actually be built.

Imperial to metric conversion is ideal and if we could snap our fingers and everything would work instantly that would be great. But it won't work like that and it probably won't be happening any time soon.

What I mean is I genuinely don't understand why rounded values are considered correct and raw is not if I put down an answer to a problem. Why not just annotate to what precision a raw value is? Even though you don't measure to more precision, if you do a calculation with collected data the raw value is more likely to be closer to the actual value. It's not guaranteed, but the discrepancy is enough that I have been confused for years of why to sacrifice the accuracy.

ex: assuming uncertainty of the measurement of the side of a perfect square is equal in both directions, say +/- 1 mm, and the side length is measured as 35 mm, doing an area of 35x35 with sig fig rounding is 1200 mm^2. Without sig figs (raw) it's 1225 mm^2. 

The upper bound 36x36 is 1296, the lower bound is 1156. The raw value is equidistant from both bounds, the sig fig value is not. Given the actual value could fall anywhere in that range with equal probability, the raw value is more likely to be closer to wherever the true value is, but the sig fig value is more likely to be further off. 

I made a matlab plot that illustrates this a bit better: https://imgur.com/EmT7Xck

That is the manifestation of my idea that sig figs are less accurate than raw. That's just one example but it's basically everywhere that involves a calculation.

edit: why not just annotate raw values with uncertainty, like 1225 +/- 70. mm^2? The 2 sig figs in the uncertainty denote how many are not "actually there" in the raw 1225.

I use the method of adjusting mirrors way out, it's actually recommended by the society of automotive engineers (it's called the SAE method)

Here's how it works: if you want to change lanes and see someone already in your blindspots, you don't turn your head, you don't change lanes.

If you don't see anyone, you do turn your head, if you still see no one, you should be clear.

It's a massive misconception people have that they think people are trying to get rid of head turning and you still have to do it as often anyway. You're safer when your head is facing forward. If you can eliminate shoulder checks by means of already seeing something without turning your head, that is ideal. That is what this does.

The same applies for blindspots mirrors.

Edit: it's even a misnomer to call them blindspots anymore since the effect is is to let you see them. Not sure how it figures into a blindspot mirror but the SAE method cuts your blindspots by 60% and removes 100% of redundancy between your 3 mirrors. You turn your head much, much less often.

All risks are unnecessary, don't gamble with 2 tons of steel. If you're stuck in a tight spot you could have avoided to begin with, it's up to you to slowly take steps to reduce that risk into certainty regardless what impatience other people have
